title: Where did all the sitcoms go?

summary.quality_note: This digest explains why sitcoms are less common now, based on a conversation with Mike Schur, a TV show creator. It's a good example of how economics and technology can change industries.
summary.headline: Why Are There Fewer Sitcoms on TV Now?
summary.tldr: Streaming services have changed how TV shows are made and sold, making it harder for sitcoms to be profitable. This has led to fewer sitcoms being created, even though they are still popular with audiences.

key_points.point: Sitcoms used to be a big part of TV, but now they make up less than 2% of new shows in the 2020s, down from 12% in the 1990s.
key_points.why_it_matters: This shows a big shift in what kinds of TV shows are being made.

key_points.point: In the past, sitcoms could lose money on their first run but still make money later through syndication (reruns on other channels).
key_points.why_it_matters: This gave creators a chance to recoup costs over time.

key_points.point: Streaming services usually buy fewer episodes of a show, which makes each episode more expensive to produce.
key_points.why_it_matters: This changes how TV studios calculate their costs and profits.

key_points.point: Streaming services value shows based on how many minutes people watch, not how many people watch them. This makes sitcoms (which are shorter) less valuable.
key_points.why_it_matters: This affects what kinds of shows are made and how they are structured.

key_points.point: Comedies often need time to develop and find their rhythm, but streaming services want shows to be successful quickly.
key_points.why_it_matters: This makes it harder for sitcoms to succeed in the streaming era.

summary.lesson: The way TV is made and sold has changed a lot with the rise of streaming services. These changes have made it harder for sitcoms to be profitable, even though they are still popular with audiences.
opinions_and_predictions: Mike Schur said that the economics of TV have changed dramatically in the last 15 years, and one of the casualties has been the comedy.
Mike Schur said that it's unlikely anyone would be able to make a sitcom the old way, with 22 episodes and a casual hangout format, in today's market.
Mike Schur said that the streaming world system does not give comedies the time they need to experiment and find their footing.

glossary.definition: When reruns of a TV show are sold to other channels for broadcasting, usually after the show has finished its initial run on a network or streaming service. This can be a way for studios to make money from a show long after it has been created.
glossary.example: Shows like Seinfeld and The Office became very popular through syndication.

glossary.definition: An accounting principle where the cost of a large purchase is spread out over time. In TV production, this means spreading the cost of making a show over the number of episodes.
glossary.example: If a set costs $3 million, it might be spread over 22 episodes, but now it might be spread over 8 episodes, making each episode more expensive.
